title: Asymmetric proxy scheduling + application-level pacing experiments (notes)
body:
Purpose and quick summary:

This is a working log of experiments that tried to reproduce, characterize, and mitigate asymmetric tail-latency induced by proxy scheduling decisions when clients send bursty streaming requests. The main observation we chased: small, client-side bursts (microbursts) + per-connection fairness in upstream proxy scheduling causes long tails for a subset of requests even when aggregate capacity is sufficient. Application-level pacing (coarse client-side rate smoothing) dramatically reduces P99 tails for streaming workloads, but it interacts non-trivially with gRPC flow-control and HTTP chunking semantics.

Why this matters to Redwood:
- Streaming generation and chat workloads are often characterized by many small writes followed by long polling for tokens (client-side chunked inputs or tool-calls).
- Tail latency increases directly degrade UX and can cascade into higher token costs due to retransmissions or duplicate requests.
- Customers moving to Dedicated/Private often place proxies in front of runtime; we need robust guidance and defaults.

Hypotheses we tested:
1) Proxy scheduling that enforces per-connection fairness (round-robin dequeue per socket) amplifies client-side microbursts into head-of-line delays for other connections behind the same proxy worker.
2) Application-level pacing (coalescing writes into fixed-duration windows) will reduce microburst-induced queueing and thus tail latency without hurting median latency if configured correctly.
3) gRPC over HTTP/2 behaves differently than HTTP/1.1 chunked POST for small-chunk streaming because of HTTP/2 flow control and prioritization; gRPC can either help or hurt depending on window sizing and prioritization algorithm at the proxy.

Testbed / env details:
- Proxy: edge-proxy (in-house) v0.54 w/ default scheduler (per-connection round-robin). Test branch included a scheduler toggle patch from PR 245.
- Backend: serving-runtime worker (same binary used in pre-prod) pinned to a single GPU; model small/medium transformer serving with fixed short-generation work (mean 80-200 tokens).
- Client generator: custom harness (wrk2 + python driver) capable of sending N concurrent long-lived streaming connections; supports both HTTP/1.1 chunked and gRPC streaming modes and client-side pacing knobs.
- Network: single AZ, 10Gbps NICs; artificially introduced 2ms baseline latency and 0.1% packet loss in some runs to simulate WAN-ish conditions.
- Socket settings toggled: TCP_NODELAY on/off, TCP_CORK on/off on client and proxy; socket rmem/wmem tuned in some experiments.
- Key metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency to first token and to last token, CPU utilization (proxy and backend), proxy queue depth per-worker, socket write syscall rate, retransmits, and gRPC window update rate.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Traffic shapes: steady open-connections (N=500) with periodic small 1–3 chunk bursts; high concurrency bursts (flash 1k connections); single big request baseline.
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1 chunked POST vs gRPC bidi-streaming.
- Scheduler modes: per-connection RR (default), per-request fair-queueing (new mode), and worker-coalescing (batching dequeues per-worker).
- Client pacing: none (baseline), micro-pacing 2–10ms write spacing, coalesce-window 20–50ms, and token-based batching (collect up to K bytes then flush).

Key findings (summary):
1) Default per-connection RR scheduler + client microbursts => bimodal tail distribution. A small fraction (~3–7%) of streams experienced 4–10x higher tail latency compared to median. These were correlated with connections that happened to arrive right after a proxy worker drained a large request.
2) Turning on coalesce-window (20–30ms) in the client reduced P99 to ~0.5–0.7x of baseline in most steady-state experiments. Median latency unchanged. The improvement tracked strongly with reduced syscall write-rate (fewer small writes) and lower proxy queue head-count variance.
3) gRPC over HTTP/2: when HTTP/2 initial window was small (default), gRPC streams saw increased stalling (backpressure) at the proxy; increasing window_size on proxy->backend reduced stall events but increased proxy memory. HTTP/1.1 chunking had simpler behavior: microbursts were visible but easier to mitigate with client coalescing because each chunk translated to a single request-body write (no per-stream flow control).
4) Scheduler change to per-request fair-queueing flattened tail latency distribution significantly (P99 reduced by ~30–60%) but increased median latency slightly in some high-concurrency runs due to scheduling overhead. Worker-coalescing (batch dequeues) achieved much of the benefit with lower overhead.
5) TCP/Nagle (TCP_NODELAY off + TCP_CORK style coalescing) on client helped a bit when OS-level coalescing was allowed; on the proxy we saw mixed results — enabling coalescing reduced write syscall pressure but added 1–3ms of packetization delay which harmed MNs for very low-latency flows.

Representative numbers (steady chat-like workload: 500 streams, 1–3 small chunks per message):
- Baseline (per-conn RR + no pace): p50=18ms, p95=62ms, p99=220ms
- Client 25ms coalesce-window: p50=18ms, p95=58ms, p99=95ms
- Scheduler=per-request fair-queue: p50=20ms, p95=50ms, p99=80ms
- gRPC (default window) baseline: p50=22ms, p95=75ms, p99=300ms
- gRPC (window=256KB): p50=21ms, p95=60ms, p99=110ms

Micro-observations and traces:
- Traces show many proxy-workers entering short-lived bursts where dequeue loops handle a hot connection that keeps producing small bodies; other connections stuck behind the worker's loop until it yields. This confirms hypothesis #1.
- Socket-level traces: when client wrote many small fragments, proxy had ~3–6x increase in sys_write calls and higher scheduler wakeups; the backend queue (per-worker) saw spiky enqueue times.
- RTT breakdown: the extra P99 mass is dominated by queueing inside the proxy (not GPU inference or network). CPU samples at the proxy showed time spent in copying small buffers and scheduling overhead.

Practical mitigation options tested:
1) Client-side: default recommendation for SDKs — enable a light coalescing buffer (10–30ms) for streaming writes and/or flush-on-final-chunk only. Provide SDK knob: StreamingWrite.coalesce_ms.
2) Proxy-level: implement worker-coalescing dequeue (batch up to M requests per-worker loop) + a max-dequeue time to avoid hogging. This preserved throughput and flattened tails.
3) Flow-control tuning: for gRPC, recommend increasing initial window for higher-concurrency streaming customers or enable dynamic window growth for long-lived streams.
4) Socket heuristics: prefer leaving TCP_NODELAY on for ultra-low-latency single-chunk flows, but allow TCP coalescing heuristics on when the client is known to send many small writes (SDK can set flags based on pattern).
5) Scheduling policy: expose an operator-configurable default to Dedicated customers: per-request fair-queueing for latency-sensitive clusters, worker-coalescing for throughput-optimized clusters.

Trade-offs and concerns:
- Coalescing increases end-to-end latency for the first token by the coalescing window; we observed this to be negligible at p50 for 20–30ms but could be problematic for sub-10ms SLOs.
- Larger HTTP/2 windows reduce stalls but increase memory overhead on proxies and backend (per-stream buffers). For very high fan-out customers this can impact memory headroom.
- More complex proxy scheduling adds CPU overhead; we need to benchmark at scale (10k+ concurrent streams) to ensure cost economics hold.

Action items / next experiments:
- (Aisha) Build a small SDK patch to add StreamingWrite.coalesce_ms with opt-in default = 25ms for server-streaming and bidi cases. Test with real web SDKs. Target: prototype by 2026-07-30.
- (Miguel) Run scaled worker-coalescing experiment across 5-node cluster (10k concurrent streams) and measure CPU/memory tradeoffs. Target: 2026-07-28. JIRA-RT-1127.
- (Rina) Add an e2e test in CI that exercises gRPC window-size permutations and flags potential memory pressure. Link to PR: github.com/redwood-repo/edge-proxy/pull/245.
- (Benji) Instrument proxy to export per-worker dequeue-batch-size and head-of-queue hold-time metric to Grafana. Quick dashboard by 2026-08-05.

Notes to product / SRE / docs:
- Product: consider adding a default note in Dedicated onboarding recommending a "Streaming pacing" SDK setting, with explanation of trade-offs and typical recommended values (10/25/50ms presets).
- SRE: provide a runbook for diagnosing proxy-induced tail spikes: look at per-worker queue-length variance, syscall write rate, and gRPC window update counters.
- Docs: add a short appendix in "Networking and streaming" guide that describes interaction of HTTP/2 window, proxy scheduling, and SDK pacing.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How do these results change for cross-region clouds where network RTT is 30–100ms? My suspicion: relative benefit of client coalescing will be smaller but worker-level scheduling will still cause relative tail amplification. Need targeted WAN experiments.
- Could kernel-bypass network stacks (DPDK/accelerators) change these characteristics dramatically? Possibly — they could shift bottleneck from syscall overhead to application scheduling.
- Is there a safe auto-tuning rule for coalesce_ms in SDKs (based on observed write burstiness)? We should prototype heuristics (e.g., detect >X writes within Yms => enable coalescing).

Appendix: quick checklist when reproducing locally:
- Ensure proxy build has both scheduler modes toggles (env flags: PROXY_SCHED=per_conn|per_req|coalesce).
- Use client harness with precise timing (hw clock aligned) — python sleep has jitter; use nanosleep or high-res timers.
- Collect: p50/p95/p99 for first-token and last-token, per-worker dequeue histograms, syscall write counts, gRPC window-update counters.

If you want raw experiment logs / sample flamegraphs ping me and I'll drop them into Confluence (CON-4832) or attach to JIRA-RT-1127.

-- Aisha
